messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David, a 56-year-old guitarist who had spent three decades commanding stages, now found his world had shrunk to the four walls of his home studio. The trauma had occurred eight months ago, after a show. An influential promoter, a man whose authority in the local music scene was absolute, had invited him for a "private drink" to discuss a tour. The meeting had ended in a violent sexual assault. The promoter’s expensive cologne, a cloyingly sweet scent, had filled the small office. In the struggle, David had hit his head against the desk, the coppery taste of blood in his mouth as he was overpowered. This event shattered not just his sense of safety, but the very narrative of his own life.

The memory of that night never arrives as a coherent story. Instead, it surfaces in vicious, sensory fragments. Some moments are appallingly clear: the specific pattern on the office carpet, the glint of a watch on the promoter’s wrist. Other parts are a complete blank, a black hole where the worst of the violence resides. He finds himself constantly pushing the memory away before it can fully form, a desperate mental flinching. When these shards of memory do break through—the scent of the cologne, the feeling of being pinned down—they bring with them an overwhelming conviction that he is in imminent danger, as if the assault is happening all over again in the present moment. This terror is so profound that his only response is to retreat. He cancels meetings with agents, avoids old friends from the music scene he used to see after gigs, and has essentially become a recluse, his world contracting to only the places he deems safe.

His pervasive sense of threat has become the lens through which he views the world. A sudden movement from his wife in the kitchen puts him instantly on guard, his body tensing for a blow. This constant hypervigilance makes it impossible for him to relax enough to let the memory of the assault be processed; any feeling of being unsafe causes his mind to slam the door shut on the past. The feeling of being perpetually endangered also primes him to notice potential threats everywhere. The scent of a floral perfume on a passerby, for instance, is no longer just a smell but an alarm bell that signals imminent harm, sending him into a state of high alert. This constant state of threat has fueled a deep, simmering irritability that he fights to control. He feels a hot rage just beneath the surface but has come to believe that expressing it would be catastrophic, so he swallows it down, a decision that leaves his jaw perpetually aching.

This strategy of suppressing his anger and avoiding all reminders of the trauma has only tightened its grip. By refusing to engage with anyone in a position of authority, he has sabotaged his own career, turning down opportunities that would have once been the lifeblood of his work. His avoidance of old social contacts has left him profoundly isolated, which in turn makes any accidental encounter with a former friend feel intensely triggering and dangerous. Furthermore, these efforts to avoid and suppress have kept the traumatic memory itself in a state of suspended horror. Because he never allows himself to fully recall what happened, it remains a collection of terrifying fragments, each one capable of ambushing him without warning, reinforcing the idea that the world is an unsafe place and that he is fundamentally broken. A movie scene depicting violence can send him fleeing the room, heart pounding, as it connects directly back to the unprocessed core of his own experience.

It was an outburst last week that finally brought David to seek help. His wife, reaching quickly for a dropped glass, made a sudden movement that triggered an explosive, aggressive reaction from him. He didn't touch her, but his shout was so full of raw fury that it left them both shaking. The look of fear in her eyes was more than he could bear. He realized that in his desperate attempt to keep himself safe, he had made his own home, the last safe place on earth, feel dangerous for the person he loved most. He came to therapy not with a clear goal, but with a desperate, fragmented plea: to be able to sit in a room with his wife without flinching, and to one day tell a clear story of what happened, even if only to himself.
